title: Lifshitz-Kosevich Theory of Anomalous Landau Levels in Topological Flat Bands
abstract: In conventional metals, quantum oscillations arise from Landau quantization of Fermi-surface cyclotron orbits, whose dynamics are governed by the Fermi velocity and cyclotron effective mass within Lifshitz-Kosevich (LK) theory. A perfectly flat band, by contrast, has vanishing group velocity, which would naively imply an infinite cyclotron mass and complete thermal suppression of quantum oscillations. Yet topological flat bands can support anomalous Landau levels (LLs) whose finite-field spacing is generated by quantum geometry rather than band curvature, allowing quantum oscillations to persist. This work addresses how such anomalous flat-band LLs behave within the LK framework and whether their thermal damping can reveal quantum geometric information. Using a minimal model with exactly flat topological bands, we derive an LK theory for these anomalous LLs and analyze fixed-density magnetization oscillations. The resulting oscillations exhibit a finite LK effective mass that is substantially larger than the normal-band value and possesses a strong magnetic-field dependence. In the weak-field limit, this anomalous mass reflects the quantum geometric origin of the LL spacing and scales inversely with both the magnetic field and the trace of the quantum metric. Thus, thermal damping of flat-band quantum oscillations directly measures the quantum metric, establishing quantum oscillations as a probe to flat-band quantum geometry.
summary: This work develops an extension of Lifshitz-Kosevich theory to describe quantum oscillations arising from anomalous Landau levels found in topological flat bands. By analyzing the temperature dependence of these oscillations, the authors demonstrate that the thermal damping factor yields a measurable effective mass directly proportional to the system's underlying quantum geometric structure.
main_problem: To determine how quantum oscillations persist in topological flat bands, which naively suggest thermal suppression due to zero group velocity, and whether the thermal damping factor can reveal information about the underlying quantum geometry.
main_result: The paper derives an LK theory for anomalous Landau levels (ALLs), showing that their persistent oscillations yield a finite, field-dependent effective mass whose thermal damping directly measures the quantum metric of the flat band.
method: The authors adapt the Lifshitz-Kosevich formalism to analyze the grand potential and magnetization oscillations in the presence of an anomalous LL spacing. They fit temperature dependence using standard LK forms to extract effective masses.
model_or_system: The study uses a minimal model Hamiltonian describing topological flat bands, relevant to moiré materials, which possess Time-Reversal and inversion symmetries. The analysis is performed under a perpendicular magnetic field at fixed carrier density.
key_observables: Magnetization ($M$) oscillations as a function of $1/B$, the extracted effective mass ($m^*_{	ext{eff}}$), and the thermal damping factor derived from the fundamental harmonic amplitude ($A_1(T)$).
important_parameters: Magnetic field ($B$), temperature ($T$), carrier density ($ho$), and parameters related to the quantum metric tensor.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a minimal model with perfectly flat topological bands, and it treats the local LK fit as a diagnostic tool for measuring the effective mass derived from thermal damping.
figures_summary: Figures show band dispersion, Berry curvature distribution, LL spectra, and magnetization oscillations ($M$ vs $1/B$) for both normal and anomalous LLs. Subsequent figures compare extracted effective masses against analytical expectations.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem by contrasting conventional Landau quantization with flat bands. It then adapts the LK formalism to derive oscillatory terms ($\delta\Omega$), analyzes the thermal damping factor ($R_T(p)$), and finally extracts the field-dependent effective mass, linking it theoretically to the quantum metric.
why_interesting: The direct link established between measurable transport properties (thermal damping of oscillations) and fundamental geometric invariants (the quantum metric) provides a powerful new experimental probe for characterizing topological band structures in condensed matter systems.
